title: Every crash window
objective: For each crash window, with and without provider idempotency, produce the shortest trace to a double charge or a lost intent, or "none", and name its class; then show a duplicate that needs no crash.

blocks.md:
Between a customer's click and a settled charge, your system takes five steps, and a crash can land between any two of them. In some gaps a crash only delays the charge. In others it double-charges, or loses the charge, or does nothing at all. You will place the crash yourself, then ask TLC.

One prediction first. In the time stage you wrote the claim CL-5.2, and its model sent the provider request in the same step that changed the hold. When those two steps come apart, which part of that claim cracks: the proposition of the model, the correspondence, the requirement fit, or an assumption record? Keep your answer. The lesson returns to it.

choice.prompt: No crash happens. Your worker's timer fires before the provider's reply arrives, and it sends again. The provider ignores keys. Can the charge happen twice?

options.text: No: without a crash there is nothing to retry.
options.why: Timers retry too, and a slow reply looks exactly like a lost one.

options.text: Yes.
options.why: Both copies can be accepted. At-least-once delivery duplicates by design.

options.text: Only if the network duplicates the message.
options.why: Your own re-send creates the duplicate. The network need not.

choice.prompt: Your worker stored the provider's result, then crashed before it marked the intent done. On restart, what should it do?

options.text: Send again: the intent is not acknowledged.
options.why: The stored result proves the effect happened. Sending again turns this window into a double charge.

options.text: Drop it: the provider already has it.
options.why: The intent would stay inflight forever, and nothing would record that it finished.

options.text: Acknowledge it from the stored result.
options.why: Recovery reads what is durable before it acts.

blocks.md:
A command's chain has four gaps where a crash matters. Call them windows.

| Window | A crash lands between | One crash here permits |
|---|---|---|
| CW1 | Commit and Dispatch | delay only: the intent waits in the outbox |
| CW2 | Dispatch and Accept | you place the crash |
| CW3 | Accept and Persist | you place the crash |
| CW4 | Persist and Ack | you place the crash |

CW1 is the worked example. Commit writes the command and its pending intent. The worker crashes before it sends anything. Recover restarts it, the intent is still pending, Dispatch sends one request, the provider accepts it, and one charge happens. The answer for CW1 is none. You complete the other three in the Theater, with provider idempotency off, and the table fills in as you go.
Enable one window, crash, recover and continue by hand. The monitors count charges per command.
blocks.direction: Scene asserts: no command is charged more than once. The monitor counts the provider's charges for each command as you play, and marks a second one.

code.text:
InWindow(w, c) ==
  CASE w = "CW1" -> status[c] = "pending"
    [] w = "CW2" -> /\ status[c] = "inflight"
                    /\ \E r \in reqs : r.cmd = c
                    /\ ~\E r \in replies : r.cmd = c
    [] w = "CW3" -> /\ \E r \in replies : r.cmd = c
                    /\ c \notin durable
    [] w = "CW4" -> c \in durable /\ status[c] = "inflight"
    [] OTHER     -> FALSE

\* A crash empties the worker's memory. The database and the network are not the worker's to lose.
Crash == /\ up
         /\ CrashBudget
         /\ \E c \in committed, w \in CrashWindows : InWindow(w, c)
         /\ up' = FALSE
         /\ got' = {}
         /\ crashes' = IF MaxCrashes < 0 THEN crashes ELSE crashes + 1
         /\ UNCHANGED <<committed, status, durable, attempts, reqs, replies, charges, seen>>

\* Recovery returns every inflight intent without a stored result to pending.
Recover == /\ ~up
           /\ up' = TRUE
           /\ status' = [c \in Cmds |-> IF status[c] = "inflight" /\ c \notin durable
                                          THEN "pending" ELSE status[c]]
           /\ UNCHANGED <<committed, durable, attempts, got, reqs, replies, charges, seen, crashes>>

call.prompt: Window CW2: the crash lands after your worker sent the request and before the provider accepted it. Can a double charge follow?

options.text: No: the provider never saw the first request.
options.why: It has not seen it yet. That copy is still in flight and can arrive after the re-send.

options.text: Only if the provider crashes too.
options.why: The provider stays up in this scene. Delay alone is enough.

options.text: Yes: both copies can be accepted.
options.why: Recovery re-sends, and the old copy is still deliverable.

blocks.after: TLC finds the same thing: `NoDoubleCharge` fails in CW2, and the run records the witness and its length in actions {{run:RUN-tlc-double-charge}}. The provider accepted nothing before the crash, yet the retry still double-charges, because the first copy was never lost. Try CW3 and CW4 the same way, and fill in the rest of the table.

choice.prompt: Provider idempotency off, one command, one crash, allowed only in CW3. Which is the shortest trace to a double charge?

options.text: Commit, Dispatch, Accept, Receive, Crash, Recover, Dispatch, Accept.
options.why: It double-charges, but Receive is not needed, so a shorter trace exists.

options.text: Commit, Dispatch, Accept, Crash, Recover, Dispatch, Accept.
options.why: The worker crashed before it stored the reply, so recovery treats the intent as unanswered and re-sends. The provider has no memory of the key and performs the effect again.

options.text: Commit, Dispatch, Accept, Crash, Recover, Accept.
options.why: A second charge needs a second request, and only the worker's re-send makes one.

options.text: None: the provider performed the effect only once.
options.why: One accepted request is one charge. The re-send after recovery is the second.

blocks.md:
Now ask TLC the same question. The Bench runs TLC on the same model with one worker and the deadlock check off, because a finished command is not a deadlock. On a phone you see the recorded run with its id.

Run CW3 with provider idempotency off first. TLC reports that `NoDoubleCharge` fails and prints a trace like the one you just built {{run:RUN-tlc-double-charge}}. That trace is specimen SP-8.1: the first copy was accepted, the worker crashed before it stored the reply, and the re-send made a second charge.

Then run the full design: every window, two crashes, and a provider that honors one stable key per intent.

blocks.direction: Check asserts: all four invariants hold in every reachable state. An error means some behavior violates one. A clean finish means none does, at these constants.

code.text:
java -jar tla2tools.jar -workers 1 -deadlock -config Outbox_full.cfg Outbox.tla

CONSTANTS Cmds = {c1}  MaxCrashes = 2  MaxAttempts = 3  CrashWindows = {"CW1", "CW2", "CW3", "CW4"}
          Dedup = TRUE  FreshKey = FALSE  Forgets = "never"  Timeouts = FALSE
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT NoLostIntent
INVARIANT AckedIsDurable
INVARIANT NoDoubleCharge

options.text: A violation: some window still double-charges.
options.why: One stable key plus the provider's idempotency closes CW2 and CW3, and recovery closes CW4. The provider's idempotency is part of this model.

options.text: No error, and the exploration completes.
options.why: Every reachable state satisfies all three, at these constants.

options.text: It stops early and reports a deadlock.
options.why: This configuration turns the deadlock check off on purpose.

blocks.after: TLC reports no error and finishes exploring. The stamp is MODEL-CHECKED [M] · constants · complete {{run:RUN-tlc-outbox-safety}}. Read the constants beside it: one command, two crashes, a provider that honors keys and never prunes them. Change one of those and you have a different claim.

blocks.md:
Compare the run with the answer you kept. SP-8.1 cracks an assumption you wrote in the time stage: that the provider request left in the same step as the hold's commit. This is SEAM-4, and it was never true of a system that calls an outside service. `res <= 1` still holds on the old model. What fails is the assumption that the effect left with the commit, so the part that cracks is an assumption record. Three remedies follow: an outbox, built here; inbound keys, next lesson; and the provider's idempotency, stated as an assumption in CL-8.2.

NoLostIntent, checked with crash actions on, is your first claim of this stage. It rests on two assumptions: the command and its intent commit together, and a crash loses memory only.

choice.prompt: After a crash and a recovery, the worker is up. The database holds a stored result for the command, its intent is still inflight, and no reply is in the worker's memory. Which of Dispatch, Receive, Persist, Ack and Recover are enabled?

options.text: Dispatch and Ack.
options.why: Recovery returned only intents without a stored result to pending. This one stays inflight.

options.text: Receive, Persist and Ack.
options.why: The reply sat in the worker's memory, and a crash emptied it. Receive is also off once a result is stored.

options.text: Ack only.
options.why: With a stored result, Ack is enabled and Dispatch is not. Recovery acts on what is durable.

segments.title: A poller and a late commit

blocks.md: A crash is not the only way an effect fails to leave. Many systems deliver outbox rows with a poller. It reads committed rows above a high-water mark, delivers them, and raises the mark to the highest id it read. Two writers take sequence ids when they INSERT, and they commit in either order.
Drive the writers and the poller by hand and watch the mark.
blocks.direction: Scene asserts: every committed row is delivered, and the mark never passes a committed row that was not delivered.

code.text:
Insert(w) == /\ wpc[w] = "idle"
             /\ idOf' = [idOf EXCEPT ![w] = nextId]
             /\ nextId' = nextId + 1
             /\ wpc' = [wpc EXCEPT ![w] = "inserted"]
             /\ UNCHANGED <<committedIds, delivered, mark>>

CommitRow(w) == /\ wpc[w] = "inserted"
                /\ committedIds' = committedIds \cup {idOf[w]}
                /\ wpc' = [wpc EXCEPT ![w] = "committed"]
                /\ UNCHANGED <<nextId, idOf, delivered, mark>>

\* Design "mark": rows above the mark.  Design "status": rows not yet delivered.
Batch == IF Design = "mark" THEN {i \in committedIds : i > mark}
                            ELSE committedIds \ delivered

Poll == /\ Batch /= {}
        /\ delivered' = delivered \cup Batch
        /\ mark' = IF Design = "mark" THEN Max(Batch \cup {mark}) ELSE mark
        /\ UNCHANGED <<nextId, idOf, wpc, committedIds>>

MarkInv == \A i \in committedIds : i <= mark => i \in delivered

call.prompt: Writer 1 takes id 1. Writer 2 takes id 2 and commits first. The poller delivers row 2 and sets its mark to 2. Then writer 1 commits. Will row 1 be delivered?

options.text: No, never.
options.why: Ids are allocated at INSERT and become visible at COMMIT, so id order is not commit order. Row 1 sits below the mark.

options.text: Yes, on the next poll.
options.why: The next poll reads ids above 2, and row 1 is below the mark.

options.text: Yes, after the worker restarts.
options.why: The mark is stored, and a restart reads it back.

blocks.after: The mark invariant fails. With weak fairness on the poller, eventual delivery fails too, on a lasso that stutters after the last poll {{run:RUN-tlc-lost-effect}}. This is specimen SP-8.2. PostgreSQL records the same late commit: poll 1 delivers id 2 and moves the mark to 2, the first transaction then commits, and poll 2 returns no rows, at every isolation level (row H20 {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}}).

blocks.md: Poll by status, not by id. Claim pending rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and delivery stays at-least-once. The [PostgreSQL 18 documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-select.html) says that skipping locked rows "provides an inconsistent view of the data": it claims rows, and it never promises completeness.

choice.prompt: A poller claims pending rows by status instead of by id. Two writers insert and commit in either order, and polls run in between. Can a committed row be skipped forever?

options.text: Yes: writer 2 commits first, a poll delivers row 2, then row 1 commits below the mark.
options.why: That trace belongs to the mark design. This poller has no mark to fall behind.

options.text: No: a committed row stays pending until a poll claims it, whatever the commit order.
options.why: Pending is a property of the row, not of its id, so a late commit is claimed by the next poll.

options.text: Only when the writers commit in id order.
options.why: Commit order does not matter here. Status decides what a poll claims.

choice.prompt: Provider idempotency off, timers on, crashes off, one command. Which is the shortest trace to a double charge?

options.text: Commit, Dispatch, Timeout, Dispatch, Accept, Accept.
options.why: The timer returns the unanswered intent to pending, and the worker sends again while the first copy is in flight.

options.text: None: with no crash, nothing is sent twice.
options.why: A timer fires on a slow reply just as it does on a lost one.

options.text: Commit, Dispatch, Accept, Accept.
options.why: Each request copy is accepted once. A second accept needs a second request.

choice.prompt: Two commands, c1 and c2, one crash, allowed only in CW4. The provider ignores keys. Which trace is a behavior of the model?

options.text: Commit c1, Dispatch c1, Accept, Receive c1, Persist c1, Crash, Recover, Dispatch c1.
options.why: Recovery does not return an intent with a stored result to pending, so Dispatch is not enabled.

options.text: Commit c1, Dispatch c1, Accept, Ack c1.
options.why: Ack needs a stored result, and only Persist writes one.

options.text: Commit c1, Commit c2, Dispatch c1, Accept, Receive c1, Persist c1, Crash, Recover, Ack c1.
options.why: The crash lands in CW4 for c1. Recovery leaves its stored result alone, so Ack is enabled.

options.text: Dispatch c1, Commit c1, Accept, Receive c1, Persist c1, Ack c1.
options.why: Dispatch needs a pending intent, and only Commit writes one.

blocks.md: The tablespace course takes the same reasoning one layer down (its durability material, T3), where a write-ahead log decides what survives and the harness, not timing, enumerates the crash points. Drawer D-12 is its one-page prerequisite.

blocks.title: TigerBeetle: reliable transaction submission
blocks.md: TigerBeetle's page "Reliable Transaction Submission" (read 2026-10-23), the sections "Handling Network Failures" and "Handling Client Software Restarts": the client generates the id, persists it "before submitting the transfer", resends with the same id, and a duplicate returns `exists`. The pins are in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}. Trace three questions against your table: which of CW1 to CW3 persisting first closes, what a resend after a client restart looks like, and which result says an earlier attempt was accepted.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: [PostgreSQL 18 documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/) (read 2026-10-21): SELECT, The Locking Clause; Sequence Manipulation Functions, whose values are "not reclaimed" on abort.

ROW H01 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: both commit, final 20, the second debit's write returns 20 -> 20. SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, is recorded: 40001.
ROW H02 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the waiting statement updates 0 rows. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, are recorded: 40001.
ROW H03 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the DELETE removes 0 rows and a hits = 10 row exists before and after. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H04 [agrees]: The reader's two reads total 250 at READ COMMITTED and 200 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H05 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ with a team total of -100; at SERIALIZABLE the second committer fails with 40001 and the total is 50.
ROW H06 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ (160 held against 100); at SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001 and 80 stays held.
ROW H07 [agrees]: Run from the upstream specs: REPEATABLE READ gives s3 a state no serial order shows; SERIALIZABLE aborts s2 with 40001 (-2); DEFERRABLE makes s3 wait (-3).
ROW H08 [agrees]: 6 of 210 permutations fail with s3 READ ONLY; the READ WRITE variant is measured here, not read from the spec comment.
ROW H09 [agrees]: The second count is 3 at READ COMMITTED, 2 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H10 [agrees]: With one session SERIALIZABLE and the other READ COMMITTED both commit, in both assignments and both commit orders; with both SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001.
ROW H11 [agrees]: A sequential scan aborts a SERIALIZABLE transaction that shares no row with the other; the same transactions on an index scan over distant keys both commit.

ROW H12 [agrees, with additions]: 23505 and 23P01 appear under SERIALIZABLE; which of 40001 and 23505 appears depends on whether the failing session checked first and on the order, and a whole-command retry with a re-check ends without error where a blind retry fails again.
ROW H13 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the statement waits, then updates the row it could not see. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H14 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: 23505, no restart. REPEATABLE READ: 23505. SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H15 [agrees]: Disjoint claims at all three levels; the count through SKIP LOCKED is 0 while 4 jobs are pending.
ROW H16 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED returns the rows out of order; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE raise 40001; FOR UPDATE in a subquery returns them in order.
ROW H17 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: mallory sees 'secret from mallory'. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: her locking read fails with 40001, so it is prevented by failure.
ROW H18 [agrees]: CHECK accepts NULL, the guarded UPDATE skips the NULL row, USING hides it, WITH CHECK raises 42501; the same at all three levels.
ROW H19 [agrees]: 22003 'bigint out of range' at all three levels; the balance is unchanged; sum(bigint) is numeric.
ROW H20 [agrees]: Row 1 is never delivered: the mark is 2, both ids exist, the next poll returns nothing; the same at all three levels.
ROW H21 [agrees]: Both permutations of the regression test end with bar's 40001, the output the upstream file expects.

ROW H22 [differs]: Ascending order removes the deadlock and both commit at READ COMMITTED. At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, 4 of the 6 ascending-order permutations still fail with 40001 (first updater wins), so ordering is no substitute for the retry.
ROW H23 [agrees]: B's COMMIT fails with 40001; its retry reads 20 available, the guard refuses (0 rows) and nothing is written.
ROW H24 [agrees]: REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: B fails with 40001 and its retry updates 0 rows. READ COMMITTED: no error, 0 rows.
notes: The tester is PostgreSQL's own isolationtester, built from the 18.6 source tarball and run against the Debian-packaged 18.6 server of the postgres:18 image; it is not statespace isorun (W4-T16).

isolationtester prints errors as 'ERROR:  <message>' without a SQLSTATE. SQLSTATEs come from the server's csv log: each session's application_name is '<tag>/<session>', and for every session the messages the tester printed must equal the messages the server logged, in order; a mismatch stops the run.
NULL prints as an empty cell in isolationtester output; an empty string prints the same way.

A session that continues after an error meets 'current transaction is aborted' (25P02) at its next write. Those follow-on errors stay in the row outputs, as after_abort in the index, and keep a history out of the GEN-anomaly-id pool.
The lock model that decides which interleavings cannot hang the tester is sound and incomplete; every lock wait the tester reported was one the model predicted.
The grid's 'half' split, the target counts and the retry patterns are design defaults [D], not measurements.
Nothing was emulated: no browser, phone, hosted service or other PostgreSQL version was involved. PGlite is a different instrument (W0-S08).

notes: Recorded by W1 follow-up 1 (task_label W1-followup-1); the task field is left out because run@1 accepts only W<n>-S<nn> or W<n>-T<nn> there.
A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
Isabelle is developed in Mercurial; the pin is from its GitHub mirror, isabelle-prover/mirror-isabelle.
input sha256 for each command is the SHA-256 of the lines it printed, joined by newlines with a trailing newline.
